title: Paul VI's pilgrimage to the Holy Land
shortBlurb: Pope Paul VI landed at Amman and entered Jerusalem, the first pope to leave Italy in more than a century and a half and the first to come to the Holy Land since St. Peter…
body: On 4 January 1964 Pope Paul VI landed at Amman, where King Hussein of Jordan received him, and travelled on to Jerusalem, entering the Old City by the Damascus Gate. His three-day pilgrimage, announced barely a month before, was the first journey of a pope outside Italy since Pius VII had been carried to France in 1809, and the first ever made by air.

He had come, he said, as a pilgrim to the places where Christ had lived. He prayed at Gethsemane and along the Via Dolorosa, celebrated Mass in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, and passed into Bethlehem; on 5 January he embraced Athenagoras, the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople, on the Mount of Olives — the first meeting of a pope and a patriarch of Constantinople since the Council of Florence in 1438.

The journey, made while the Second Vatican Council was still in session, opened the age of the travelling papacy: nine international journeys would follow in his pontificate, from Bombay to the United Nations. The embrace with Athenagoras bore fruit two years later, when Rome and Constantinople together lifted the anathemas of 1054.

sources.text: Pope Paul VI, Apostolic Pilgrimage to the Holy Land, 4-6 January 1964 (vatican.va)

title: The election of Pope St. Pius V
shortBlurb: The cardinals chose the Dominican inquisitor Michele Ghislieri, who as Pius V would press the Council of Trent's reform upon the whole Church…
body: Born Antonio Ghislieri in 1504 at Bosco, near Alessandria in Piedmont, he entered the Dominicans at fourteen, taking the name Michele, and was ordained in 1528. A strict inquisitor in Lombardy, he was made bishop of Sutri in 1556, cardinal and grand inquisitor the next year, and bishop of Mondovì in 1560. On 7 January 1566, less than a month after the death of Pius IV, the cardinals elected him pope — largely, contemporaries said, through the influence of St. Charles Borromeo — and he took the name Pius V.

He was crowned on 17 January, his sixty-second birthday, and kept his white Dominican habit, whence the pope's white cassock to this day. His six years pressed the Council of Trent's decrees into practice: the Catechism of the council appeared in 1566, the reformed Roman Breviary in 1568, and the Roman Missal in 1570, which he imposed upon the whole Latin Church.
In 1570 he excommunicated Elizabeth I of England, and in 1571 the Holy League he had welded together broke the Ottoman fleet at Lepanto. He died on 1 May 1572 and was canonized by Clement XI in 1712.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Pope St. Pius V”

title: The election of Pope Fabian
shortBlurb: A dove settling on the head of an unknown layman, as Eusebius records, marked Fabian as the Roman church's choice for its bishop…
body: After the death of Pope Anterus, who had sat barely forty days, the clergy and people of Rome assembled to choose a successor. Among them stood Fabian, a layman newly come in from the country, of whom no one had thought. In the received chronology the day was 10 January 236.

Eusebius relates that a dove suddenly descended upon Fabian's head, and that the assembly, taking the sight as a token of the Spirit's descent, chose him with one voice and set him in the chair of Peter.

His pontificate of some fourteen years fell in a lull between persecutions. The Liber Pontificalis credits him with dividing Rome into seven districts, each under a deacon; tradition sent St. Dionysius from his day to preach in Gaul; and St. Cyprian records that he condemned Privatus, a teacher of new error in Africa. He was to end as a martyr under Decius in 250.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Pope St. Fabian”
Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 20 January

title: The death of St. Paulinus of Aquileia
shortBlurb: Charlemagne's grammarian-patriarch, hammer of the Adoptionists and apostle to the Avars, died at Aquileia…
body: Born about 726 on a farm near Friuli, Paulinus tilled his father's fields yet made himself so eminent a scholar that Charlemagne styled him in a rescript Master of Grammar and Very Venerable, bestowed an estate upon him, and raised him, against his will, to the patriarchate of Aquileia.

He stood at the emperor's side in the councils of the age — Aachen in 789, Ratisbon in 792, Frankfurt in 794 — and held his own synod at Friuli, where he vindicated the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son. When Felix of Urgel taught that Christ as man was God's Son only by adoption, Paulinus refuted him in three books, and his Libellus Sacrosyllabus, approved at Frankfurt, was sent into Spain as an antidote to the spreading error.

His zeal reached beyond controversy: he preached the gospel to the pagan Carantani of Carinthia and Styria and to the Avars, and Alcuin counted him among his dearest friends. He died on 11 January, in 804 as his biographer Madrisius reckons, though some moderns give 802; Aquileia now keeps his feast on 28 January.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 28 January

title: The death of St. Benedict Biscop
shortBlurb: The founder of Wearmouth and Jarrow, who gave England stone churches, glass windows, and books, and reared the Venerable Bede, died after three years of patient sickness…
body: Born about 628 of a noble Northumbrian family — his true name was Biscop Baducing — he served as a thegn of King Oswiu before renouncing the world at twenty-five for the first of five journeys to Rome. He took the monastic habit at Lérins, and in 668 Pope Vitalian sent him to guide Theodore of Tarsus, the new archbishop, to Canterbury.

King Ecgfrith gave him seventy hides of land at the mouth of the Wear, where in 674 he founded the monastery of St. Peter, Wearmouth, and forty more on the Tyne, where arose St. Paul's, Jarrow. From Gaul he brought masons to build in stone after the Roman fashion and glaziers, for the making of glass was then unknown in Britain; from Rome, books, relics, and pictures.

His library made possible the learning of Bede, whom he received as a boy of seven. Worn by a three-year palsy, he appointed Ceolfrith abbot of both houses and died on 12 January 690; the English Benedictines honour him as a patron of their congregation.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “St. Benedict Biscop”
Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 12 January

title: The death of St. Sava, first Archbishop of Serbia
shortBlurb: The prince-monk who won autocephaly for the Serbian Church and became her first archbishop died at Tŭrnovo on his way home from the Holy Land…
body: Born Rastko, youngest son of Stefan Nemanja, the unifier of the Serbs, he fled as a youth to Mount Athos, where he was professed a monk with the name Sava. His father followed him there as the monk Simeon, and together they founded the monastery of Hilandar, still the centre of Serbian monastic life.

Returning home about 1208 to make peace between his quarrelling brothers, Sava rebuilt the Church's life in his land; in 1219, at Nicaea, Patriarch Manuel I consecrated him the first archbishop of an autocephalous Serbian Church. He organized her dioceses, formed a native clergy, gave her the Nomocanon, and crowned his brother Stephen as king.

Resigning in 1233, he set out on a second pilgrimage to the Holy Places, and on the journey home he died at Tŭrnovo, then the Bulgarian capital, on 14 January — in 1235 as most Western accounts reckon, 1236 in the Serbian tradition, which keeps his feast on 27 January by the civil reckoning. Buried in the church of the Holy Forty Martyrs, his relics were later translated to Mileševa and burned by the Turks in 1594.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Servia”

title: The death of St. Maurus of Glanfeuil
shortBlurb: St. Benedict's first disciple, whom French tradition makes the apostle of Benedictine Gaul and the founder of Glanfeuil, died before the altar of St. Martin…
body: Maurus was twelve years old when, in 522, his father Equitius gave him to St. Benedict at Subiaco. He grew into the saint's coadjutor; St. Gregory the Great tells in his Dialogues how Maurus, sent at a word, walked upon the lake to draw out the drowning boy Placidus, and how Benedict afterwards called him to Monte Cassino about 528.

The French tradition, received in a Life written under the name of Faustus, tells that he came into Gaul in 543 and, by the liberality of King Theodebert, founded the great abbey of Glanfeuil on the Loire, afterwards called Saint-Maur-sur-Loire. Modern critics, Butler among them, judge that Life a pious forgery; yet the cult it served was ancient and real.

Resigning the abbacy in 581, he gave his last years to solitude, and died lying on sackcloth before the altar of St. Martin on 15 January 584. For fear of the Normans his relics were moved in 868 to Saint-Pierre-des-Fossés near Paris, which took from him the name Saint-Maur-des-Fossés; the English name Seymour descends from Saint Maur.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “St. Maurus”
Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 15 January

title: The first Franciscan martyrs in Morocco
shortBlurb: Five friars sent by St. Francis to preach to the Saracens were slain by the king of Morocco with his own scimitar — the first martyrs of the new order…
body: Berard, Peter, Acursius, Adjutus, and Otto were sent by St. Francis in 1219 to preach to the Muslims of the West, while he went himself to those of the East. They preached first to the Moors of Seville, suffered much, and were banished; passing thence into Morocco, they preached Christ openly in Marrakech until the judge had them twice scourged till their ribs lay bare.
Burning oil and vinegar were poured into their wounds, and their bodies rolled over sharp stones and potsherds. At length the king, taking his scimitar, clove their heads asunder on 16 January 1220.

Their relics were ransomed and are kept in the monastery of the Holy Cross at Coimbra. There the fame of their sacrifice so moved a young Augustinian canon, Ferdinand — the future St. Anthony of Padua — that he took the Franciscan habit. Their names stand in the Roman Martyrology, and Sixtus IV canonized them in 1481, the first martyrs of the order Francis had founded eleven years before.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 16 January

title: The first Church Unity Octave
shortBlurb: At a poor friary in the Hudson highlands, an Episcopalian community began eight days of prayer for the reunion of Christians — the seed of the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity…
body: On 18 January 1908, then the feast of the Chair of St. Peter, Father Paul Wattson and Mother Lurana White led their little Society of the Atonement, a Franciscan community within the Episcopal Church, in the first Church Unity Octave, closing it on 25 January, the feast of the Conversion of St. Paul. The place was Graymoor, near Garrison in New York, and Wattson spread the observance through his magazine The Lamp.

The next year the friars and sisters of Graymoor were received into the Catholic Church, and Pius X gave the octave his blessing. In 1916 Benedict XV extended it, under the name of the Chair of Unity Octave, to the whole Church.

The observance outgrew its origin: since 1968 its materials have been prepared jointly with the Faith and Order commission of the World Council of Churches, and as the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity it is kept each year between the same two feasts by Christians of every communion.

sources.text: Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, Dicastery for Promoting Christian Unity (vatican.va)

title: The martyrdom of St. Blathmac at Iona
shortBlurb: An abbot of Iona who would not betray the shrine of St. Columba to the Danish pirates was cut down at the morning Mass…
body: Blathmac, the son of an Irish king, was abbot of the monastery of Iona, the island St. Columba had made the lamp of the northern churches. The Northmen had burned Iona in 802 and slain sixty-eight of its monks in 806; the shrine of Columba had been solemnly restored in 818.

When the Danes came again, they found Blathmac celebrating the morning Mass. They demanded the shrine of St. Columba, with its gold and silver, and he, refusing to betray the treasures of the church, was struck down upon the altar steps. The Annals of Ulster record his martyrdom under 825; older writers placed it about 793, and the Catholic Encyclopedia about 835. The Irish calendars keep his memory on 19 January.

His life was written in Latin hexameters by Walafrid Strabo, abbot of Reichenau, and so the story of his witness has been handed down. The relics of Columba were at last carried to Ireland in 849 for safety, and Iona's day as the mother house of the Gaelic church drew towards its close.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “St. Blathmac”
Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 19 January

title: The martyrdom of Pope St. Fabian
shortBlurb: The pope chosen under the sign of the dove was among the first to fall when the emperor Decius loosed his persecution upon the Church…
body: In the first days of 250 the emperor Decius commanded sacrifice to the gods throughout the empire, and the blow fell first upon the shepherds. Fabian, bishop of Rome for fourteen years, was seized and died a martyr on 20 January 250; whether by the sword or in prison, the sources leave uncertain.

St. Cyprian, writing to his successor Cornelius, called him an incomparable man, whose glory in death answered the purity and holiness of his life. He was buried in the catacomb of Callixtus on the Appian Way, where his grave slab, broken in pieces, still bears the Greek words: Fabian, bishop, martyr.

His death opened the first great test of the Church under a general persecution: the see of Rome stood vacant for more than a year while the storm raged, and when Cornelius was at last chosen, the question of those who had lapsed under the trial would divide the Church for a generation.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Pope St. Fabian”
Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 20 January

title: The martyrdom of St. Fructuosus of Tarragona
shortBlurb: A bishop and his two deacons were burned alive in the amphitheatre of Tarraco, the protomartyrs of Christian Spain…
body: In the persecution of Valerian, Fructuosus, bishop of Tarraco on the Catalan coast, was taken in the night of 16 January 259 with his two deacons, Augurius and Eulogius, and kept in prison five days. On 21 January they were tried by the governor Aemilianus; the bishop confessed Christ and his office — "I am a bishop," he answered, and the governor said, "You were" — and all three were sentenced to be burned alive.

Led to the amphitheatre, the bishop refused the cup of spiced wine, for it was a Wednesday and the hour of breaking the fast had not come, and declared that he must pray for the whole Catholic Church spread through east and west. When the fire had burned through their bonds, the three knelt with outstretched arms in the form of a cross and gave up their souls.

That night the faithful gathered their ashes and laid them beneath the altar. Their acts are among the most genuine of antiquity: St. Augustine preached their praise in a sermon that survives, and the poet Prudentius sang them in his Peristephanon.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “St. Fructuosus of Tarragona”
Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 21 January

title: The founding of Georgetown College
shortBlurb: On a hilltop above the Potomac, John Carroll secured the ground for the first Catholic institution of higher learning in the United States…
body: Under colonial law Catholics in America had been forbidden to conduct schools; the Revolution made a Catholic college possible. John Carroll of Maryland, a former Jesuit and from 1784 the head of the American missions, had planned such an academy with his fellow clergy since 1783, published his Proposals in 1786, and seen building begun in 1788.

On 23 January 1789 Carroll received the first deed for the hilltop property at Georgetown, above the Potomac — the date the university still keeps as its founding. In the same year he was chosen the first bishop of the United States.

The college welcomed its first student, William Gaston, in November 1791, and instruction began the following January; from 1805 it has been directed by the Society of Jesus; and in 1815 an act of Congress signed by President Madison granted its charter. It remains the oldest Catholic university in the country.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Georgetown University”

title: The translation of St. John Chrysostom's relics
shortBlurb: Thirty years after the golden-mouthed preacher died in exile, his relics came home to Constantinople in a procession of imperial repentance…
body: St. John Chrysostom had died at Comana in Pontus on 14 September 407, exiled by the court whose vices he had rebuked, his last words a doxology: Glory be to God for all things. Thirty years later his disciple Proclus, then patriarch, preached his praise in Constantinople until the people begged for the relics' return.

The emperor Theodosius II sent envoys with a silver reliquary to Comana, and, since his mother Eudoxia had driven John into exile, wrote with his own hand a letter asking the saint's forgiveness. The relics were borne to the capital with the utmost pomp, the emperor and his sister Pulcheria walking in the procession and begging pardon for the sins of their parents.

They were laid in the Church of the Holy Apostles, the burying-place of emperors and bishops, on 27 January 438 — the day on which the Latin Church long kept his feast, while the Greeks kept 13 November. In 1204 the crusaders carried much of the treasure westward to Rome.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “St. John Chrysostom”
Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 27 January

title: The death of Pope Gelasius II at Cluny
shortBlurb: Hunted from Rome by the emperor's faction, Pope Gelasius II died in exile at Cluny after a pontificate of a single year…
body: John of Gaeta, a monk of Monte Cassino, had been made cardinal in 1088 and chancellor in 1089 by Urban II, and had served Paschal II in the same office. On 24 January 1118 the cardinals chose him pope as Gelasius II — and that very night the Frangipani, the emperor's allies in Rome, seized and maltreated him until the people broke in and set him free.

He fled to Gaeta, where he was ordained priest and consecrated bishop in March, while Henry V set up the excommunicated archbishop of Braga as the antipope Gregory VIII. From Capua that April Gelasius excommunicated the emperor and his creature, and when Rome could no longer hold him he sailed by Pisa into France.

He reached the abbey of Cluny and died there on 29 January 1119, having suffered more in one year, his contemporaries said, than any pope since the age of the martyrs. The cardinals with him chose Callixtus II in the same abbey on 2 February, and three years later the Concordat of Worms brought the long struggle over investiture towards its end.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Pope Gelasius II”

title: The death of St. Aldegundis of Maubeuge
shortBlurb: The Merovingian princess who founded the double monastery of Maubeuge and bore slander and cancer without complaint died on 30 January…
body: Aldegundis was born about 630 in Hainault, the daughter of Walbert, of the Merovingian royal blood, and of Bertilia, and sister of St. Waldetrudis of Mons. Consecrating herself to God in her youth, she resisted every suit of marriage, and in 638 took the religious veil and founded at Maubeuge, on the Sambre, a great double house of virgins which she governed as its first abbess.

Her life was a hidden one of prayer, tried by violent slanders and, at the end, by a lingering cancer of the breast, whose tortures — the caustics and incisions of the surgeons — she bore, Butler says, not only with patience but with joy.

She died on 30 January, in 684 as most modern accounts reckon, though Butler, following the Bollandists, gives 660. Her relics were enshrined at Maubeuge; her name stands on this day in the martyrologies of Rabanus Maurus, Usuard, and Notker, and in the Roman Martyrology; and she is invoked as a patroness of those who suffer from cancer.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 30 January

title: The death of St. Maedoc of Ferns
shortBlurb: The pupil of St. David who became the first bishop of Ferns and one of the fathers of the Leinster church died on 31 January…
body: Maedoc — called also Aidan, and in the endearments of Irish speech Mogue and Maodhog — was born in Connacht about the middle of the sixth century. Passing into Wales, he lived long under the direction of the holy abbot David at Menevia, and returned to Ireland with a company of monks of eminent piety.

He founded many churches and monasteries, the chief about 598 at Ferns in the Wexford country, on land granted in the territory of the Ui Cheinnselaig, and was made its first bishop; the monastic school there became one of the glories of the Leinster church.

He died on 31 January, in 632 as Ussher reckons, though the annals are divided between 624 and 632. His feast was kept in Wales in the twelfth century, as Giraldus witnesses, and in Scotland the chronicle of Scone and the Aberdeen breviary prayed for the divine mercy through his intercession. He remains the patron of the diocese of Ferns.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 31 January
